extracted.intended_audience: educated eighteenth-century readers; writers and critics of prose and poetry; general public interested in morals and literary taste
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short didactic essays and literary criticism that give moral instruction and guide taste in poetry and conduct; mixes prescriptive advice about character, social conduct, and poetic technique for a general reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity must rest upon frugality
rubrics_metrics.description: All Liberality should have for its Basis and Support Frugality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be generous only within means so that benevolence is sustainable; avoid sacrificing future ability to do good by unguarded, impulsive largesse. Ensure charity flows from reasoned conviction, not passion; do not reduce one's fortune below capacity to act according to one's natural temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial benignity as an everyday habit
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant Benignity in Commerce with the rest of the World, which ought to run through all a Man's Actions, has Effects more useful to those whom you oblige, and less ostentatious in your self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In buying, selling, lending and neighbourly acts be just, easy, and averse to disputes; such steady kindness does greater good than occasional ostentatious gifts and allows liberal behaviour without exhausting personal fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal charitable acts to avoid envy
rubrics_metrics.description: Among Traders, he who obliges is as much concerned to keep the Favour a Secret, as he who receives it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep acts of assistance discreet to prevent creating enemies or provoking envy; publicising benefactions may make them invidious and diminish their social value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target support to the industrious and deserving
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of supporting good and industrious Men would carry a Man further even to his Profit, than indulging the Propensity of serving and obliging the Fortunate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lending and assistance aimed at industrious, upright persons (who may be rescued from bankruptcy) rather than favouring already-fortunate individuals; such targeted benignity benefits society and may repay the benefactor materially and reputationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend benevolence via public investment
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Nation where there are so many publick Funds to be supported, ... he who does not embark some part of his Fortune with the State cannot be called a good Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing part of one's wealth in public funds or supporting state finance is a means of laying obligations on many and extending beneficence widely; it's a civic form of benignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay excessive praise until a life is complete
rubrics_metrics.description: We are naturally averse to the launching out into a Man's Praise till his Head is laid in the Dust. Death only closes a Man's Reputation, and determines it as good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in lavish or premature praise because a person's life may change and deeds may later contradict present admiration; reputation is properly sealed by the whole course and end of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency — a good death should fit a good life
rubrics_metrics.description: The End of a Man's Life is often compared to the winding up of a well-written Play, where the principal Persons still act in Character, whatever the Fate is which they undergo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value uniformity of conduct: dying 'in character' (steady courage, piety, cheerfulness consistent with life) is a confirmation of a well-lived life; authenticity in last moments is praiseworthy but must correspond to a well-spent life to be truly admirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and measured expression indicate true greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty is the certain Indication of a great Spirit... He that writes with Judgment, and never rises into improper Warmths, manifests the true Force of Genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bombast and affectation; restrained, well-judged expression betrays real talent and greatness, whether in conduct or in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: True courage must be allied with justice and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage, without regard to Justice and Humanity, was no other than the Fierceness of a wild Beast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate bravery not merely by bold action but by the presence of reason, honour, duty, and humane motives; courage exercised without moral compass is merely ferocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine magnanimity from ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Affectation of such a Spirit exerts itself in an Impudent Aspect, an over-bearing Confidence, and a certain Negligence of giving Offence... A shameless Fellow takes advantage of Merit clothed with Modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of noisy, ostentatious displays of 'courage' or wit—such affectation is inferior to quiet, genuine resolution and can mask smallness of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public praise provokes detractors and can suppress talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit, both as to Wit and Beauty, is become no other than the Possession of a few trifling Peoples Favour... There is a vicious Terror of being blamed in some well-inclin'd People, and a wicked Pleasure in suppressing them in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise social dynamics: conspicuous praise often invites malice, and fear of scandal may deter capable people from displaying their talents; moderation and discretion in commendation may protect reputations and foster talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poets may embellish scant tradition with invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If we look into the three great Heroick Poems ... they are built upon very slight Foundations... afforded him an Opportunity of embellishing it with Fiction, and giving a full range to his own Invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When historical or traditional material is sparse, a poet may reasonably add invention and circumstance to produce a satisfying epic, so long as the principal particulars generally believed in tradition are respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve essential traditional character traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil has... preserved this Character in the Person of Æneas... the Character of Æneas is filled with Piety to the Gods, and a superstitious Observation of Prodigies, Oracles, and Predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting legendary material, maintain core character traits transmitted by tradition (e.g., Æneas's piety); incorporate traditional elements (prophecies, oracles) where they underpin the character's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualify or contextualise ludicrous or incredible incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: That ludicrous Prophecy ... which one of the Harpyes pronounces ... many Readers have been shocked... but when they hear that this was one of the Circumstances ... they will think the Poet did very well in taking notice of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle potentially ridiculous details by situating them appropriately (e.g., spoken by a comic or child character) or by prefacing them with justification (appeal to tradition), so they read as natural within the poem rather than absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use framing and speaker choice to make odd lines acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an observation, which is beautiful in the Mouth of a Boy, would have been ridiculous from any other of the Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign lines or prophecies to suitable speakers (a boy, a hungry Harpy, etc.) whose perspective renders the line plausible and artistically effective; this preserves sense and avoids inappropriate seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance heroic qualities across characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If Equipage and Address make Turnus appear more couragious than Æneas, Conduct and Success prove Æneas more valiant than Turnus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic valorization: portray characters with a range of qualities (piety, conduct, success, ostentation) and let different virtues be weighed (apparent bravery vs steadfastness and rightful conduct) in assessing heroism.
